title: Row Minimum That Tops Its Column
statement:
You get an m × n grid matrix of distinct integers. A value is special when it is the smallest in its row and, at the same time, the largest in its column.

Return every special value. Any order is accepted.

examples.why: 6 is the smallest in the bottom row and the largest in the first column. The row minimum 4 loses its column to 6, and 1 loses its column to 12.
The row minimums are 3 and 2, but 9 beats 3 in its column and 8 beats 2 in its column.
A single cell is both the smallest of its row and the largest of its column.

hints: Checking one cell needs the minimum of its row and the maximum of its column. Can you compute all of those once instead of per cell?
Collect the minimum of every row and the maximum of every column. A special value must appear in both collections.
Because values are distinct, there can be at most one special value. Try to prove it: if two existed, compare them through the cell where one's row meets the other's column.

explain.intuition:
The test for one cell is two scans: its row and its column. Doing that for every cell repeats the same work many times. Instead, compute every row minimum and every column maximum once, then keep the values that show up in both lists.

There is a neat bonus: with distinct values, at most one special value can exist. Say x sits at (r1, c1) and y at (r2, c2). Look at the cell (r1, c2): it is at least x (x is its row minimum) and at most y (y is its column maximum), so x < y. The cell (r2, c1) gives y < x the same way. Both cannot hold. So the answer is the largest row minimum, if it is also the smallest column maximum.
steps: Put the column maximums into a set.
Return every row minimum that is also in that set.
pitfalls: Returning every row minimum, or every column maximum, without checking the other condition.
Comparing the row minimum with the maximum of the wrong column: the check is against the column where that minimum actually sits. With distinct values, set membership handles this automatically.
Recomputing the column maximum inside the cell loop, which turns an O(m·n) job into O(m·n·(m + n)).

solutions.title: Check every cell
solutions.idea: For each cell, scan its row and its column and keep it if it wins both comparisons.

solutions.title: Row minimums meet column maximums
solutions.idea: Compute all row minimums and column maximums once; the answer is their intersection.

followups: Prove that at most one special value exists, and use that to return a single number in O(m·n) time and O(1) extra space.
What changes if values may repeat? Can there now be several special values?
